name: Beth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest, I nearly didn't come, because these things usually end with someone selling me an app. But the kids are at swimming till six, so you've got me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a stockwoman on Hollins Farm, about 400 hectares, owned by the Pryce family. I'm out at half six to check the suckler cows and the ewes, then feeding, bedding, foot trimming, whatever the day throws at me, and the barley and rape in between when they need hands. I keep my calving records in a red notebook, because I've never trusted a screen with a living thing. What wears me out is February, when you're up at night with heifers and still expected at the grain store at eight.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Dev, who drives the big tractor and sprays, and we eat our sandwiches in the grain store most days. Owen Pryce, the owner's son, does the office side, the forms and the computer stuff. I've been there fourteen years, my partner Marco fixes buses for the county, and we've a mortgage on a terrace on Mill Lane with our two, Lila and Ben.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the grain store for two years: it's hype. Dev would laugh, because I told him the self-driving tractor salesman was full of it. Online I don't post much, but I might share something from the union about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job and I sleep fine. The pay on Hollins is good for farm work, we've got a good few months saved and Mum's money from when she passed sitting in the building society. If the computers stay stupid, my red calving notebook and I are safe on Hollins Farm for another twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep paying my union dues, because that's what kept our pay decent when the Pryces wanted to cut overtime in 2022. If there's spare, Marco and I would put an extra hundred a month on the mortgage so it's done before the kids leave school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a breath out. A bit smug, if I'm honest. I don't like being told the world's changing when all I can see is the same cows needing the same care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Owen does the computer side. What does he use now, and would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He has a program for the cattle passports and the grain contracts, and I think he's tried one of those chat things for writing letters to the bank. In this picture he might save an hour a week on forms. That doesn't touch me, because no program has ever pulled a calf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind about work or money, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, which I know is lucky. My back twinges in winter, and old Mr Pryce is seventy-four, so one day the farm passes to Owen. But Owen likes me and the farm makes money, and there are three other farms within ten miles that would take me tomorrow.

say: I'd tell Dev in the grain store that **AI is hype**, like the self-driving tractor salesman.
I'd share a **union post** online rather than write anything myself.
think: My job on Hollins Farm feels **safe for twenty years** if the computers stay stupid.
We have **good savings** and Mum's money, so money isn't a worry.
do: Keep paying **union dues**, because the union protected our overtime pay in 2022.
Put an extra **£100 a month** on the mortgage so it's clear before the kids leave school.
feel: Relieved and a bit **smug**, because the change never looked real from the cattle shed.
S0.quote: If the computers stay stupid, my red calving notebook and I are safe on Hollins Farm for another twenty years.
fieldNote: Beth trusts a **paper notebook** over any screen and says so with pride.
Her calm rests on **real security**: good pay, savings, an inheritance and farms nearby that would hire her.
She already watches the **succession** from old Mr Pryce to Owen, but doesn't see it as a threat.

steps.text: Keep the same stock job on Hollins Farm and the red notebook
Overpay the Mill Lane mortgage by £100 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, let the office have it, the cows still need me. With the union I'd say we need rules on what bosses can do with all the data these programs collect on us. I'd probably grumble about it at the school gate too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Owen would buy one of those herd systems with collars that flag a sick cow, and then expect me to carry a tablet around. I'd hate that. My job's still there, but it would start to feel like I'm working for the screen instead of the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ring Karen, our union rep, and ask what the agreement says about new tech and training on paid time. I'd keep doing the job the way I do it and only use the tablet when Owen makes me. And I'd keep the extra mortgage money going, maybe bump it to two hundred, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared for my wage, but it's like someone moving the furniture in your own house while you're out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the day Owen hands you that tablet. What happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thanks and put it in the Land Rover's glovebox, and I'd keep the red notebook going. If the collar says cow 214 is off her food, fine, but I'll have spotted her standing at the back of the yard first. Owen would sigh, and we'd muddle along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, more than me. A lot of his spraying and drilling is already done by the GPS, and if the planning goes to a program, the Pryces might decide one tractor driver can cover two farms. Dev has a new baby and no savings, so I'd be pushing the union hard for Dev before I pushed for myself.

say: I'd tell work the **cows still need me**, so let the office have the software.
I'd say through the union that bosses need **rules on data** these programs collect.
think: Owen would likely buy **cow collars** and hand me a tablet I don't want.
My **wage is safe**, but the work would start to feel like serving a screen.
do: Ring **Karen, the union rep**, about training on paid time and new tech rules.
Raise the mortgage overpayment to **£200 a month** as a precaution.
Use the tablet **only when told** and keep the red notebook going.
feel: Uneasy, like someone **moving the furniture** in her own house while she's out.
S1.quote: Dev has a new baby and no savings, so I'd be pushing the union hard for Dev before I pushed for myself.
fieldNote: Her own income looks safe; her unease is about **losing control** of how she works.
She worries more for **Dev**, a colleague with a new baby and no savings.
Resistance shows as **quiet refusal**: the tablet goes in the glovebox.

steps.text: Carry on the stock work and keep the paper calving records
Ask the union rep to secure paid training and data rules
Raise the mortgage overpayment to £200 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd be at the union meeting saying we need a law before 2031, not after. Online I'd share every petition going, and at work I'd tell Owen to his face that the people who built this farm deserve better than a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished on Hollins by 2031. The office goes in 2028, which won't hurt me much, but three years later a robot that can trim feet and calve heifers is cheaper than me. Fourteen years I've been learning to spot a sick cow a day early, and a machine will learn the same trick in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the mortgage overpayments and build cash instead, because cash is what you need when the wage stops. We'd cut the holiday to the coast and the second car. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal: notice, a year's pay, and first refusal on any job minding the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. Angry too. I lie awake thinking about Lila, who wants to be a vet, and wondering if that's even a job by the time she's twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives in 2028 and the robots around 2031. What do those three years in between mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are my warning. The office side changes first, so Owen will be planning everything with the AI, and he'll see on his screen exactly what I cost. I'd use those years to save hard and get the union deal signed before the robots arrive in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said plenty of farms nearby would take you. Does that still help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if they all buy the same robot. Those farms are only a safety net while farms still need people. Marco's in the same boat at the bus depot, so we'd both be looking at the same few years, which is what frightens me.

say: I'd tell the union we need **a law before 2031**, not after.
I'd tell Owen to his face that **workers built this farm**, not robots.
think: I expect to be **out by 2031**, when robots can trim feet and calve.
Nearby farms are **no safety net** if they all buy the same robot.
do: Stop mortgage overpayments and **build cash** for when the wage stops.
Cut the **coast holiday** and sell the second car this year.
Push the union for **a year's pay** and first refusal on machine-minding jobs.
feel: Sick and **angry**, lying awake over the family's future.
Afraid for **Lila**, who wants to be a vet.
S2.quote: Fourteen years I've been learning to spot a sick cow a day early, and a machine will learn the same trick in a week.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year gap** as a countdown, not a reprieve.
Strong savings soften the blow but she still expects to **lose her wage** and maybe Marco's too.
She blames **owners and tech firms** and turns straight to the union and the law.

steps.text: Switch mortgage overpayments into a cash savings account
Cut the coast holiday and sell the second car
Push the union for a year's pay and first refusal on machine jobs
Sign and share petitions for a robot law before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but calmer: we've got five years to make rules, so let's not waste them. I'd want the union going to our MP now, not in 2033. With friends I'd say it's coming, and the people who own the land will do very well out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd still lose the job, just later, around 2034 when the robots come. I'd be fifty-one. That's old enough that nobody retrains you, young enough that you've got fifteen years of bills left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep overpaying the mortgage, because by 2034 I think we could have Mill Lane paid off if we're tight. I'd go on the union's farm committee, which I've always said no to. Marco's talked about doing a heating engineer course, and I'd tell him to do it now while I'm still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can work on. Five years is enough to get the house clear, and a house with no mortgage is a lot of peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on. With AGI in 2031 and robots in 2034, which part of your day changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and the paperwork, which is mostly Owen's anyway: when to wean, what to feed, which cows to sell. He'd ask the computer instead of asking me, and that stings a bit, because he used to come to me. Then three years later the hands part goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never retrain. Is that still true with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I'm not going to sit in front of a screen at fifty learning to boss robots. If somebody has to retrain in our house, it should be Marco, because Marco can learn anything with an engine in it.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to make rules, so don't waste them.
I'd tell friends the **landowners** will do very well out of it.
think: I'd still **lose the job**, just later, around 2034 at fifty-one.
Fifty-one is too old to retrain and too young to **stop paying bills**.
do: Keep overpaying so the **Mill Lane mortgage** is clear by 2034.
Join the **union's farm committee**, which I've always turned down.
Push Marco to start the **heating engineer course** now while I earn.
feel: Worried, but it's a worry she **can work on**.
Comforted by the idea of a **house with no mortgage**.
S3.quote: If somebody has to retrain in our house, it should be Marco, because Marco can learn anything with an engine in it.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from alarm to a **concrete plan**: clear the house.
She feels slighted that Owen would **ask the computer** instead of her.
Retraining is something she pushes onto **Marco**, not herself.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage to clear Mill Lane by 2034
Join the union's farm committee and lobby the local MP
Help Marco sign up for a heating engineer course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for a decent government to sort it, so there's no excuse. I'd be campaigning for a fund paid by the big landowners to look after farm workers. People at the school gate would get sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd ride it out longer than most. Robots in 2039 means I'm fifty-six, the house is paid for, and I'd have a pension pot that's not bad. It's Lila and Ben I'd really worry for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Hollins and keep the union stuff going. Marco and I would sit down and work out if I could stop at fifty-six and live off his wage and savings till the pension. And I'd talk to Lila about vet school properly, because vets still have to put a hand on an animal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more for the kids than for me. It's a strange feeling, planning to be pushed out and calling it retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lila and Ben about their future in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to pick work where you have to be in the room with someone, a person or an animal. And I'd tell them to join a union the day they start work. I'd tell my daughter Lila to become a vet anyway, because a sick dog's owner will still want a human hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd plan to stop at fifty-six. Is that a choice or a push?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A push dressed up as a choice, if I'm honest. I'd rather work till sixty-five on that farm. But I'd rather leave with my head up than be told to go by a man with a spreadsheet.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves a decent government no excuse.
I'd campaign for a **landowner-paid fund** to look after farm workers.
think: Robots in 2039 leave me at **fifty-six** with the house paid off.
My real worry is for **Lila and Ben**, not for myself.
do: Work out with Marco whether I can **stop at fifty-six**.
Keep **union campaigning** going for a fund for displaced farm workers.
Talk to Lila properly about **vet school** and hands-on careers.
feel: Anxious, more for **the kids** than herself.
Uneasy about calling being pushed out **retirement**.
S4.quote: I'd tell my daughter Lila to become a vet anyway, because a sick dog's owner will still want a human hand.
fieldNote: She still expects to lose her farm income, just at **fifty-six** instead of fifty-one.
Her answer to a decade's warning is to plan an **early exit** on her own terms.
Her career advice to the children is about **human contact** and unions.

steps.text: Plan with Marco to stop farm work at fifty-six
Campaign through the union for a landowner-paid farm worker fund
Help Lila plan for vet school and hands-on careers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because I'd lose the job at forty-eight with the house half paid. What would help is a law that says if a farm brings in robots, the workers get a year's pay and first refusal on the new jobs. And a proper union deal on Hollins before any of it starts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but who notices the cow standing at the back of the yard? Nobody has ever paid me for knowing which cow will be sick tomorrow, and that knowing is the real job.

headlineQuote: Nobody has ever paid me for knowing which cow will be sick tomorrow, and that knowing is the real job.
portrait: Beth is a **stockwoman** on Hollins Farm with fourteen years' service, paper records and a strong union card.
She is **secure in money**: good pay, savings, an inheritance and farms nearby hiring.
She sees **AI Plateau** as proof of hype and Steady Disruption as an annoying tablet.
In the AGI pictures she expects to **lose her job** when robots arrive and turns to the union.
More warning lets her **clear the mortgage** and plan an exit at fifty-six.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, losing the job at forty-eight with the house half paid.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** giving farm workers a year's pay and first refusal on new jobs.
A **union deal** on Hollins Farm signed before robots arrive.
